Read About Hurghada

A Red Sea city best understood through the changing relationship between reef, resort strip, working neighbourhood and desert.

FROM FISHING SETTLEMENT TO RED SEA BASE

Hurghada began as a small fishing settlement and grew rapidly with tourism along Egypt’s Red Sea coast. The result is not one compact historic centre but a long urban ribbon: older El Dahar in the north, busy Sakala around Sheraton Road and the marina, and a resort corridor stretching south along Al Mamsha.

That shape explains why the city rewards deliberate planning. A morning in El Dahar feels different from an evening on the marina, while the beaches and hotels create their own self-contained rhythm between them.

Hurghada is less a single centre than a sequence of coastal worlds stitched together by the Red Sea.

THE REEF SETS THE CLOCK

The sea is the centre of gravity. Giftun Island boat trips, Orange Bay landings and reef stops are governed by wind, visibility and marine conditions, so a sensible itinerary protects one full day and keeps its exact sequence flexible. A crew safety briefing and the day’s conditions always outrank a fixed plan.

Reef care is practical travel behaviour. Do not stand on coral, touch marine life or feed fish. Use secure sun protection, keep a dry bag with you when leaving the boat and confirm the return berth before departure.

THE OTHER HURGHADA IS INLAND

Just beyond the coastal strip, the Eastern Desert changes the scale of the journey. The mountain plain, Bedouin communities and the guided Red Sea Mountain Trail show a landscape that cannot be read from a beach lounger. Heat, dust and access rules make local guidance part of the experience rather than an optional extra.

North of Hurghada, El Gouna offers another contrast: a planned lagoon town with marinas, pedestrian pockets and wind-sports beaches. Together, these places make the city work as a base for a varied five-day stay rather than only a resort stop.
